summary: Discovery with Helionix: primary focus on hitting a 250ms-ish p95 for streaming token events across 100-150 concurrent sessions. Discussed tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted (cost-flexible, fallback routing) vs Dedicated (predictable throughput) vs Private/VPC (compliance). Agreed to run a benchmark with provided traces and share SE runbook.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
security: SOC2, KMS, SSO, audit logs
transcript: [00:00] Meeting header: 2027-05-20 16:00 UTC | Duration 52m | Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Sofia Alvarez (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (CTO, Helionix), Elena Novak (ML Lead), Marcus Green (Platform)
[00:12] Jordan Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick agenda — understand your p95 targets, concurrency shape, and then map hosting options. Sofia will walk through benchmarking steps.

[00:30] Ravi Patel: Thanks. To set context, our product streams sensor summaries in real time to operators. We're seeing spikes during fleet updates — sometimes 120 to 140 concurrent sessions, bursts up to 400 for a few seconds. Our goal: p95 end-to-end < 250ms for tokenized streaming responses, ideally at 100-150 sustained concurrency.

[01:02] Sofia Alvarez: Got it. When you say 250ms p95, is that token-to-token streaming latency or end-to-end including network? We generally break it down — inference generation p95, network RTT, and client-side processing.
[01:20] Elena Novak: We mean server-side generation + request/response handling. Network is part but we can measure separately. We have good peering in us-west and eu-west.

[01:45] Marcus Green: For network, we run through our VPC in GCP with private peering. If private deployment's easier from a latency predictability standpoint, we're open to dedicated or private options.

[02:10] Jordan Kim: Okay. High level — hosted is fastest to stand up and cheaper for low steady-state but can have more variance in p95 during cloud-wide spikes. Dedicated gives fixed capacity with predictable p95 and throughput. Private/VPC on-prem gives you control over network and security but cost and ops overhead are higher.

[02:45] Sofia Alvarez: On the serving side, main levers are batching, continuous KV cache/prefix cache, and kernel selection. For streaming low-latency targets, we often avoid big batches. Instead we rely on micro-batching and caching to amortize costs while keeping p95 low.
[03:18] Ravi Patel: Quick question — how much does KV cache actually help for streaming telemetry where prompts are mostly unique? We don't have a lot of repeating prefixes.

[03:40] Sofia Alvarez: If there's low prefix repetition, KV cache benefits drop. But we can use partial caching for common system messages or instruction prefixes. Also, batching at small sizes (2-6) can help on throughput without adding >30-40ms tail in many cases.

[04:05] Elena Novak: We measured in-house a baseline model returning ~20 tok/sec per GPU with our current infra — but that was non-streaming and single-threaded. We need better numbers for streaming behavior.

[04:30] Jordan Kim: For streaming, per-stream tokens/sec looks different. On our Hosted (default medium) profile, we typically see 15-50 tok/sec depending on model size; p95 per-token latency varies by model and sequence length. We can share a model-performance table.

[05:00] Sofia Alvarez: Also important — concurrency doesn't scale linearly with tokens/sec. If you have 150 concurrent streams each producing 10 tok/sec, that's 1500 tok/sec aggregate. That dictates GPU pool sizing or Dedicated capacity.
[05:25] Marcus Green: Right, so if we target 250ms p95 per token and have an average of 12 tok/sec per stream, how do we translate that into number of GPUs or dedicated slots?

[05:48] Sofia Alvarez: We'll need the workload traces. Rough heuristic: for an Llama2-13B-like open model, a single A100-equivalent on our runtime can sustain X streams at Y tok/sec with p95 under target — we'll run numbers in the benchmarking runbook. But I don't want to give a single-number estimate without traces and sequence length distribution.
[06:20] Ravi Patel: Understood. What's X and Y roughly? ballpark is fine.

[06:30] Sofia Alvarez: Ballpark, if streams are short-turn (10-50 tokens) and micro-batched, one A100-equivalent might handle 200-300 very-light streams at low tok/sec. But for sustained 20-30 tok/sec per stream, it drops quickly. We'll include concrete token/sec per GPU numbers in the runbook.
[07:00] Jordan Kim: Also mention quantization: if you accept a 2-3% quality delta, int8 quantization can give 1.5-2x throughput for many models which helps with aggregate tok/sec and cost.
[07:20] Elena Novak: Would quantization affect p95 or just throughput? Our concern is tail latency and hallucination risk.

[07:40] Sofia Alvarez: It mostly improves throughput; tail latency may improve since kernels are faster. Quality regressions depend on model and task — we recommend A/B evaluation. We can provision model variants for canary rollouts so you can guard quality.
[08:05] Ravi Patel: On security: we need SOC2 evidence, KMS support for keys, and SSO — SAML/SHA-2. Also audit logs for tenant activity.

[08:25] Jordan Kim: Redwood provides SOC2 reports, integrates with customer KMS for Private, and hosted supports envelope encryption with KMS. We have SAML SSO with SCIM provisioning and RBAC. I'll attach the security pack after the call (link in notes).
[08:50] Marcus Green: If we go Dedicated, can we bring our own VPC peering and route traffic directly? We care about hop counts and jitter.
[09:10] Sofia Alvarez: Yes, Dedicated supports VPC peering and private link. Private deployments give you the most control if low jitter and fixed network path are musts.
[09:40] Elena Novak: How do fallbacks work? If the primary model is saturated, will Redwood auto-fallback to a smaller, cheaper model? That could help during extreme bursts.

[09:58] Sofia Alvarez: Exactly — smart routing can fallback by policy to compatible variants (smaller or quantized) and even route to another region if you configure it. You can configure degrade-by-latency or degrade-by-cost rules. We also have canary rollouts for model changes.
[10:20] Ravi Patel: Cool. For benchmarking, what do you need from us? Traces, SLO doc — anything else?

[10:35] Sofia Alvarez: Traces with timestamps, request payload sizes, sequence length distribution, and peak concurrency windows. If you can also provide a sample of streaming session lifecycles that helps us exercise prefix caching and KV behavior.
[11:00] Jordan Kim: We'll send a short benchmark runbook and a k6 script that emulates streaming token flows. Link: https://redwood.ai/runbooks/streaming-benchmark (placeholder).
[11:20] Marcus Green: Can the k6 script show per-token arrival times? We need to map our telemetry to your input format.
[11:35] Sofia Alvarez: Yes, the script streams chunked responses and measures per-token latencies. It produces CSVs with timestamps for each token — that's what we use to compute p50/p95/p99.
[12:00] Elena Novak: Good. One more: do you do prefix or KV cache invalidation if model changes? We often update system prompts mid-release.

[12:15] Sofia Alvarez: Caches are versioned by model version and prompt hash. During rollouts, caches are warmed and old entries expire; you can configure cache TTLs and pin model versions to avoid surprises.
[12:40] Ravi Patel: Let's talk numbers. Our target is 250ms p95. What happens if hosted can't hit that under a 400 burst?

[12:55] Jordan Kim: Hosted has region-based autoscaling and fallback policies, but under extreme global surge p95 can spike. That's when Dedicated with reserved slots or elastic burst capacity helps — you get SLA-backed p95 targets agreed in contract.

[13:20] Sofia Alvarez: To add, you can set routing priorities: traffic from production route to Dedicated pool with fallback to Hosted or smaller models if Dedicated is saturated. That keeps the app live while preserving critical traffic.
[13:45] Marcus Green: For SLAs, is p95 guaranteed or is it SLO-based with credits?

[13:55] Jordan Kim: For Dedicated we offer SLA-backed uptime and latency targets — specifics depend on contract tier. Hosted has SLOs and credits for severe violations; we'll share details in the pricing doc.
[14:20] Elena Novak: Any recommendations for sequence length caps? Most of our responses are 30-120 tokens.
[14:32] Sofia Alvarez: For streaming, keeping responses under 128 tokens helps. If you have long responses, consider chunking and streaming partial answers to keep perceived latency low.
[14:55] Ravi Patel: We also throttle client-side to avoid bursts but side effects still happen when many robots update at once.

[15:05] Jordan Kim: Typical pattern is a short backoff and jitter on the client side plus server-side admission control. Redwood's runtime supports request queuing and admission to maintain p95 thresholds.
[15:30] Marcus Green: On cost — can you illustrate cost difference between hosted variable and dedicated reserved pricing for our expected load?
[15:45] Jordan Kim: We'll provide a matrix. Roughly, Dedicated reduces unit cost at scale but requires commit; Hosted is pay-as-you-go and easier for spikes. We'll send a tailored estimate.

[16:05] Sofia Alvarez: Back to benchmarking: we'll run three profiles: hosted-run baseline, dedicated-simulated (reserved capacity), and private-run (if you want on-prem profiling). Each will report p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec aggregate, and cost estimate.
[16:30] Elena Novak: How long does a run take?
[16:40] Sofia Alvarez: A meaningful run is 20-60 minutes covering representative peak and steady windows. We'll start with 20 minutes and extend if needed.
[17:00] Ravi Patel: For private deployments, what's the operational burden?

[17:12] Jordan Kim: Private requires an integration window with your infra team for VPC, KMS, and networking. We ship a control plane and optionally an on-prem runtime. There is an ops runbook and a support tier for managed updates.
[17:35] Marcus Green: We have strict data residency needs in EU — can private satisfy that?
[17:45] Jordan Kim: Yes, Private can be deployed in your EU region or on-prem. We support customer-managed KMS and audit logs for compliance.
[18:10] Elena Novak: Let's talk about measuring p95: do you include tokenization time and client assembly in your numbers?

[18:22] Sofia Alvarez: We isolate inference time from client-side assembly in the runbook. The CSV includes timestamps for request received, first token, each token emitted, and final token. You can recompute any metric you want.
[18:45] Ravi Patel: Who owns the benchmarking infra cost?

[18:55] Jordan Kim: Redwood will cover initial hosted runs and provide tools. Dedicated or Private runs on customer infra follow the agreed PO for reserved capacity; we can cost-share pilot runs for enterprise prospects.
[19:18] Marcus Green: Are there existing case studies of customers hitting similar p95 targets?
[19:28] Jordan Kim: Yes — we'll attach a short case study where a robotics fleet customer achieved ~230ms p95 for streaming with a Dedicated pool and small micro-batching plus int8 quantization.
[19:45] Elena Novak: Good to see that. Regarding observability, can we get per-token cost breakdowns? We need token-level cost for chargebacks.
[19:58] Sofia Alvarez: Yes — Redwood Console gives token-level cost, per-route and per-model. We can instrument tags for tenant and route to export to your billing system.
[20:20] Ravi Patel: Any pitfalls you've seen when customers migrate from batch to streaming?

[20:32] Sofia Alvarez: Biggest ones are missing client-side backoff, assuming linear scaling with concurrency, and not accounting for network jitter. Also, long-lived KV caches that aren't versioned can cause consistency surprises on model updates.
[20:55] Jordan Kim: We'll include an ops checklist in the runbook to help avoid those pitfalls.
[21:10] Marcus Green: About telemetry — we can redact PII and share traces. Will that be enough?
[21:22] Sofia Alvarez: Yes, trace timestamps, sequence lengths and payload sizes are the important pieces; redaction is fine.
[21:40] Elena Novak: We also want a controlled failover test where Dedicated is intentionally saturated to observe fallback behaviour.
[21:50] Sofia Alvarez: Great idea. We'll craft a failure injection scenario in the benchmark so you can confirm routing and quality degradation behaviors.
[22:10] Ravi Patel: For the follow-up SE deep dive, can we include network and infra folks? Marcus will invite VPC and security owners.
[22:20] Jordan Kim: Please do. We'll bring a solutions engineer and someone from infra to answer topology questions.
[22:45] Marcus Green: How do you handle cold starts and KV warmup? We see big tails when a new model pod spins up.
[22:58] Sofia Alvarez: Our runtime supports pre-warming and keep-alive pools. For Dedicated, you can keep a minimum number of warm workers to avoid cold starts; there's a cost tradeoff.
[23:20] Elena Novak: If we do A/B testing between quantized and full-precision models, can Redwood split traffic and measure quality regressions automatically?
[23:32] Sofia Alvarez: Yes — we support canary/A-B rollouts with automatic regression detection against your eval set and alerting for quality drops.
[23:55] Ravi Patel: Any immediate blockers you see from our side?
[24:05] Jordan Kim: Only that we need the traces and an internal SLO doc. Also confirmation of preferred region for pilot.
[24:20] Marcus Green: We'll put traces in the shared drive and confirm region is us-west2. Also will share an architecture diagram.
[24:40] Jordan Kim: Perfect. I'll send a Security pack (SOC2, PCI notes, KMS integration guide) — link placeholder: https://redwood.ai/security/helionix-pack.pdf
[25:00] Elena Novak: Can you also send the sample k6 script so we can eyeball it before you run it?
[25:10] Sofia Alvarez: Yes, will attach the script and a README explaining env vars and tokenization hooks.
[25:35] Ravi Patel: For Dedicated pricing, do you have commitment tiers?
[25:45] Jordan Kim: We do monthly and annual reserved capacity with burst options. We'll include a cost model with runbook outputs so you can see unit cost per 1M tokens.
[26:05] Marcus Green: One more technical — how do you measure model warmup effect on p95?
[26:18] Sofia Alvarez: We run phased tests: cold start burst, steady-state, and recovery windows. We track p50/p95/p99 across those phases to surface warmup tails.
[26:40] Elena Novak: Good. Does Redwood publish model kernel selection details? We want to understand sequence length heuristics.
[26:52] Jordan Kim: We publish performance profiles per model (sequence len buckets, token/sec, memory). Sofia will link the model perf table.
[27:10] Sofia Alvarez: Note that perf tables are indicative; real numbers depend on tokenization, prompt length, and concurrency pattern.
[27:30] Ravi Patel: Let's outline the pilot: 1) Helionix shares traces + SLO doc, 2) Redwood runs hosted benchmark, 3) Redwood simulates Dedicated profile, 4) review results and cost/SLAs. Agreed?
[27:52] Marcus Green: Agreed. Any business timeline constraints? We're aiming for a production decision by end of Q3 2027.
[28:05] Jordan Kim: That timeline makes sense. Pilot in next 2-3 weeks fits that.
[28:20] Elena Novak: A small request — can we get an early indicator metric after the first 20 min run rather than waiting for full analysis?
[28:33] Sofia Alvarez: Yes, we'll share quick-run dashboards and the raw CSVs immediately after the run so you can eyeball p95 behavior.
[28:55] Ravi Patel: On compliance: if we go private, do you support HSM-backed key storage?
[29:05] Jordan Kim: Yes, Private supports HSM integrations for customer-managed keys.
[29:20] Marcus Green: About monitoring — can we hook up our Prometheus stack to Redwood metrics?
[29:32] Sofia Alvarez: We export metrics and spans; we can provide a Prometheus endpoint or push via agent depending on deployment mode.
[29:55] Elena Novak: Do you support model-level throttles so we can deprioritize heavy retrieval models during peak?
[30:07] Sofia Alvarez: Yes — per-route and per-model throttles and quotas are configurable; you can also set priority classes.
[30:25] Jordan Kim: Any further questions on the hosting decision matrix?
[30:32] Ravi Patel: Just to confirm — for dedicated, SLA includes latency SLOs that we can attach to our customer contracts?
[30:42] Jordan Kim: Yes, SLA details are contract-specific but latency SLOs for Dedicated are available for enterprise tiers.
[31:00] Marcus Green: When should we expect the pricing matrix?
[31:08] Jordan Kim: I'll have a first pass by Tuesday 2027-05-25.
[31:25] Elena Novak: Can you include a column for quantized vs non-quantized performance and cost?
[31:35] Jordan Kim: Absolutely.
[31:48] Ravi Patel: Anything about regional failover — can Dedicated replicate across regions for HA?
[31:58] Sofia Alvarez: You can configure multi-region Dedicated pools and active-passive failover. Active-active is more complex but possible with traffic routing rules.
[32:20] Marcus Green: We're concerned about double billing for replication — is cross-region replication charged double?
[32:33] Jordan Kim: Replicated capacity is billed; we'll model cost tradeoffs in the pricing matrix.
[32:55] Elena Novak: On the data plane, does Redwood store any request payloads by default?
[33:05] Sofia Alvarez: For Hosted, logs are retained per your retention policy; for Private, you control data retention. We can disable request logging if required.
[33:30] Ravi Patel: Let's schedule the SE deep dive for the week of 2027-05-31. Marcus will propose times.
[33:40] Marcus Green: I'll send invites after this call. Also will include our security lead.
[34:00] Jordan Kim: Great. I'll summarize notes and post links: runbook, k6 script, security pack, model perf table.
[34:15] Elena Novak: One last technical — how do you handle tokenization differences across models during comparison?
[34:28] Sofia Alvarez: We normalize by reporting tokens per UTF-8 char metrics and map them to model tokenizers when computing token/sec so numbers are comparable.
[34:50] Ravi Patel: That should work. Any gotchas when comparing Open weights and Redwood-verified variants?
[35:00] Sofia Alvarez: Slight differences in tokenizer can skew short-response numbers; we annotate that in the perf table.
[35:20] Marcus Green: If the pilot suggests dedicated is best, what's lead time for Dedicated pool provisioning?
[35:32] Jordan Kim: For standard reserved capacity it's typically 2-4 weeks subject to contract and region availability.
[35:50] Elena Novak: And private on-prem?
[35:58] Sofia Alvarez: Private has a longer lead time — usually 6-10 weeks including network and security integration.
[36:15] Ravi Patel: Ok noted. For the benchmarking CSV, do you provide sample analyses scripts?
[36:25] Sofia Alvarez: Yes — we include analysis notebooks and a script to compute p50/p95/p99 and plot token arrival histograms.
[36:40] Marcus Green: On a related note, can you show us a sample fallback config? We want to see how graceful degradation looks.
[36:52] Jordan Kim: We'll attach a sample routing policy and an example JSON for degrade-by-latency.
[37:10] Elena Novak: Are there licensing limits on models for Private?
[37:20] Sofia Alvarez: That depends on the model licenses — for many open models it's fine; for some proprietary models, licensing restricts on-prem use. We'll flag any model-specific constraints.
[37:40] Ravi Patel: Let's confirm expected deliverables after this call: runbook + k6, security pack, pricing matrix, and a proposed schedule for the pilot. Anything else?
[37:55] Jordan Kim: Also the model perf table and a sample fallback policy. We'll include a checklist for the SE deep dive.
[38:15] Marcus Green: Sounds good. One small ask: can you include estimated token cost for our 1-hour peak scenario?
[38:27] Jordan Kim: Yes — send us the trace and we will compute cost estimates for hosted and dedicated for that peak hour.
[38:45] Elena Novak: Great. Any more questions from the Redwood side?
[38:53] Sofia Alvarez: Nothing else technical for now, we'll wait on the traces.
[39:05] Ravi Patel: Ok, we'll drop the traces in the shared folder by EOD 2027-05-21.
[39:15] Jordan Kim: Perfect. We'll aim to run the first hosted benchmark on 2027-05-22 and share early results the same day.
[39:30] Marcus Green: Quick note — our legal team will want to review SLA language; I'll loop them in after we see the pricing sheet.
[39:45] Jordan Kim: Understood — Jordan will include CRM deal id when sending materials. crm_deal_id: HXN-2027-0520 (placeholder).
[40:05] Elena Novak: Any limitations around streaming chunk sizes? We sometimes send 1-2 token chunks frequently.
[40:18] Sofia Alvarez: We support sub-token chunking via streaming APIs; extremely small chunks increase overhead but are supported. The k6 script can emulate those patterns.
[40:40] Ravi Patel: For billing, can we get per-route tagging so we can map costs to feature teams?
[40:52] Jordan Kim: Yes — tags and route-level billing are supported.
[41:10] Marcus Green: If we do private, do you provide an SLA for updates and security patches?
[41:22] Sofia Alvarez: We have a managed private support tier that includes security patch windows and scheduled upgrades; details in the enterprise support doc.
[41:45] Elena Novak: Alright. That covers most things from us.
[41:55] Ravi Patel: Thanks everyone. Quick recap?

[42:02] Jordan Kim: Recap: Redwood to share runbook, k6 script, security pack, perf table, pricing matrix. Helionix to share traces + SLO + region. Pilot scheduled: hosted run 2027-05-22, follow-up SE deep dive week of 2027-05-31. Action items captured.
[42:30] Marcus Green: I'll send calendar invites and upload traces. Expect invites from me later today.
[42:45] Jordan Kim: Great. One last thing — competitor note: if you evaluate OpenCloud AI they also support drop-in endpoints but their quantization story is less mature.
[42:58] Elena Novak: Good to know. Thanks Jordan and Sofia.
[43:10] Sofia Alvarez: Thanks all, we'll follow up with materials. Sofia signing off for the SE side.
[43:20] Ravi Patel: Appreciate the help. We'll talk soon.
[43:30] Marcus Green: Bye everyone.
[43:40] End of meeting: rough transcript produced by Fireflies.ai — some names or words may be slightly off; refer to attachments for canonical docs.
